content: No mutagenic effects were observed in the bacterial reverse mutation assay (Ames test) or the point mutation assay at the hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT) locus in V79 Chinese hamster lung cells. Similarly, no clastogenic effects were detected in vitro in the structural chromosome aberration assay in V79 Chinese hamster lung cells or in vivo in the micronucleus assay conducted on mouse bone marrow. In rats, fertility and reproductive performance were not adversely affected by cefdinir at oral doses up to 1000 mg/kg/day, which is approximately 70 times the human dose based on mg/kg/day and 11 times the human dose based on mg/m²/day. In a clinical study, cefdinir administered twice daily (BID) was compared to cefaclor 500 mg three times daily (TID). Using strict evaluability and microbiologic/clinical response criteria assessed 6 to 14 days post-therapy, clinical cure rates, microbiologic eradication rates, and statistical outcomes were determined. In a second controlled, investigator-blinded study conducted primarily in Europe, cefdinir BID was compared to amoxicillin/clavulanate 500/125 mg TID. Additionally, cefdinir was compared to a 10-day course of penicillin in adult, adolescent, and pediatric patients. Two studies (one in adults and adolescents, the other in pediatric patients) compared 10 days of cefdinir administered once daily (QD) or BID to penicillin 250 mg or 10 mg/kg four times daily (QID). Using strict evaluability and microbiologic/clinical response criteria assessed 5 to 10 days post-therapy, clinical cure rates, microbiologic eradication rates, and statistical outcomes were determined. Two additional studies (one in adults and adolescents, the other in pediatric patients) compared 5 days of cefdinir BID to 10 days of penicillin 250 mg or 10 mg/kg QID. Using strict evaluability and microbiologic/clinical response criteria assessed 4 to 10 days post-therapy, clinical cure rates, microbiologic eradication rates, and statistical outcomes were determined. Cefdinir capsules USP, 300 mg, are supplied as size ‘0’ capsules with a blue cap imprinted twice with LUPIN in black ink and a purple body imprinted twice with CEFDINIR in white ink. The capsules contain an off-white to creamish granular slug and are available in bottles of 60 capsules (NDC 68180-711-60). The capsules should be stored at 20°-25°C (68°-77°F). Patients should be counseled that cefdinir capsules, like other antibacterial drugs, should only be used to treat bacterial infections. They should be informed that cefdinir is not effective against viral infections (e.g., the common cold). When prescribed cefdinir, patients should be advised to take the medication exactly as directed, even if they feel better early in the course of therapy. Skipping doses or not completing the full course of therapy may reduce the effectiveness of the immediate treatment and increase the likelihood of bacterial resistance, making future infections harder to treat with cefdinir or other antibacterial drugs. Antacids containing magnesium or aluminum can interfere with the absorption of cefdinir. If such antacids are required during cefdinir therapy, the medication should be taken at least 2 hours before or after the antacid. Similarly, iron supplements, including multivitamins containing iron, can interfere with cefdinir absorption. If iron supplements are necessary, cefdinir should be taken at least 2 hours before or after the supplement. Diarrhea is a common side effect of antibiotics and usually resolves when the antibiotic is discontinued. However, patients should be informed that watery and bloody stools (with or without stomach cramps and fever) may occur even as late as two or more months after completing the antibiotic course. If this occurs, patients should contact their physician promptly. The interaction between alcohol and cefdinir has not been established. Patients should consult their doctor regarding the effects of consuming alcohol while taking this medication.
